And there is - a piece of cake! Or is it? To get to this point, weve assumed that there were no spelling or grammatical mistakes in the nucleotide sequence – if there were, they would have been inherited by the translation. Also that we have not verified that this is a real protein – to do, we would need to establish whether a sequence had been seen before (e.g., by searching a protein sequence database), or perhaps we would need to characterise the sequence experimentally. It's also important to understand that this particular sequence resulted from reading the sequence in a forward direction from the first nucleotide – i.e., in the first forward reading frame. It's useful to perform this analysis in all six frames in order not to miss any potential ORFs. Doing this often adds to the complexity of the result.

The reason for the relative simplicity of this is that the example comes from a prokaryotic organism – recall that prokaryotic genes don't usually have introns. So let's consider a eukaryotic sequence in which a number of introns interrupt the coding sequence (CDS). As discussed in Section 2.2.5, there are various ways to distinguish introns from exons; however, locating their boundaries is extremely difficult because the signals marking them are extremely short, and the same alphabet and words are used in coding and noncoding regions. To add an element of difficulty, consider the English text that we see in Figure 4.1(b). This time, for clarity, we've highlighted the message. As we see in Figure 4.5, this is flanked by padding words, the beginning and ends of each are marked by the shorthand device, _etc., etc., etc.. Knowing the language makes it tin bit easier to read the message

Invitably, this is a much harder problem for DNA, where language we still dont fully understand. Fortunatelyately, statistical features of the sequence, such as the GCcontent and word-usage, differ sufficiently between coding and non-coding regions to make intron-boundary detection possible. We will now put this into practice with our example eukaryotic sequence. To save time, we've already identified the start and stop codons, and have delineated the triplet words. Having done this, the interruption of the CDS (highlighted) by non-coding regions is striking, as shown in Figure 4.6(a).

Once the introns have been recognised in this way, they may be excited and the exons then shown to form a continuous gene transcript, as shown in Figure 4.6(b);
